original_article.description: Remarkable's Paper Pure replaces Remarkable 2, and it is quite good.
original_article.research:
[Lähde: TechCrunch | URL: https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/17/remarkables-new-paper-pure-is-good-thats-why-i-wrote-this-review-on-it/]
For years, the central ethos of reMarkable has been to get you away from screens and create an experience that emulates the feeling of writing with pen and paper. With its new device, the reMarkable Paper Pure, the company continues the trend of creating a device counter-positioned against phones, iPads, and laptops. As it lacks notifications and multitasking apps, the Paper Pure aims to attract writers, designers, and researchers looking for reading and writing without any distractions.

When reviewing devices, I typically write down or record notes in different forms, across different apps, and, at times, on different devices. But since this device is meant for writing, I thought it would be fitting to write the review itself on the new reMarkable Paper Pure. I have written this whole review on the tablet using its handwriting conversion feature and edited it on WordPress.

---

[Lähde: Good e-Reader | URL: https://goodereader.com/blog/reviews/full-review-of-the-remarkable-paper-pure-e-notebook]
The Remarkable Paper Pure is a highly focused, distraction-free 10.3-inch monochrome digital paper tablet that serves as the direct successor to the aging Remarkable e 2. It doubles down on the brand’s core philosophy—”notes first, distractions never”—by stripping away premium extras like color screens or front lights to deliver an exceptional, bare-bones paper writing experience at a more accessible price of $399 CAD or $399 USD for the base model, and the price goes up depending on what type of bundle you want, such as with the premium pen and a case.

The Remarkable Paper Pure is the spiritual successor to the Remarkable 2, which came out several years ago and has recently been discontinued. It features a brighter E Ink Carta 1300 screen, a much faster processor, 32GB of storage (up from 8GB), and up to 3 weeks of battery life—but it has a thicker, more plastic-heavy build than its predecessor. The Pure delivers 50% faster performance thanks to the 1.7 GHz dual-core processor and 2GB of RAM; navigating heavy PDFs and menus feels completely lag-free.

The Writing Experience: Testers from ZDNET praise the textured glass screen and active Marker Plus stylus, noting that the friction matches actual paper better than almost any tablet on the market.Lighter Form Factor: By swapping the aluminum back plate of older models for a recycled-plastic chassis, the device dropped its weight to a highly portable 360 grams.

Repairability: In line with sustainability initiatives, Engadget notes that the hardware uses screws and snaps rather than heavy adhesives, making it much easier to open and repair.

Workflow Ecosystem: The software features an incredibly clean “notes first” interface with useful background tools like calendar-linked meeting templates and smooth handwriting search.

The Remarkable Paper Pure features a 10.3-inch Canvas display based on E Ink Carta 1300. The resolution is 1872 x 1404 at 226 PPI, and this device is not a color e-note; it uses black-and-white e-paper only. It does not have a front light display, so you will have to rely on ambient lighting.

While the absence of a front light is seen as a drawback for some users reading in low light, the device has a strong appeal for purists. According to discussions on Reddit, users appreciate lower inking latency and deliberate focus on multitasking, making it an excellent tool strictly for thought and organization.

[Lähde: Engadget | URL: https://www.engadget.com/2164815/remarkable-paper-pure-review/]
There's a lot riding on reMarkable's Paper Pure, a device that has to be a lot of things to a lot of people. It's got to be a worthy replacement to 2020's reMarkable 2, the e-paper slate that made the company a household name. It needs to be a truly mass market device, or at least as mass market as a device like this can be. And it needs to woo big businesses looking for a tool it can get into the hands of hundreds or thousands of employees.

I wrote the above a full week before news broke reMarkable was slashing its workforce and firing CEO Phil Hess. According to Norway's E24, reMarkable has faced dwindling demand and rising costs thanks to the current global milieu. The Paper Pure doesn't have a lot, but in fact everything riding on its back as it makes its global debut today. Let's just hope the company's overtures toward big business don't conflict with the needs of ordinary users.

reMarkable has spent the last few years building out its high end line with the Paper Pro and Move. It's never said anything, but I get the sense both were far pricier than the company planned thanks to everything else going on right now. The flagship Paper Pro, after all, costs more than the higher-end MacBook Neo. The reMarkable Paper Pure sees the company taking what it learned from the high end and bringing it down to the rest of us.

The Paper Pure is a monochrome e-paper writing slate with a 10.3-inch display, built and priced to tempt newbies. But, the company has also got one and a half eyes on cornering the enterprise market. It measures 7.4 x 8.9 x 0.2 inches and weighs 0.79 pounds, with the left side bezel thick enough that the slate will rest comfortably in your hand. And while it's ostensibly the cheaper device, it carries the same visual design language as found on the Paper Pro line.

Inside is a 1.7GHz dual-core ARM Cortex A55, 2GB RAM, 32GB storage and a 3,820mAh battery. reMarkable says the device will last for three weeks on a charge, based on using the slate for an hour a day, every day. The 10.3-inch "Canvas" display is a customized version of E Ink's Carta 1300, which is whiter and has better contrast than the reMarkable 2.

A surprising carry over is the new Marker, which was a passive stylus on the first two reMarkable slates. They were redesigned for the Paper Pro and Move as active units, talking to their respective tablets to reduce writing latency.
